title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling, Benchmarking, and Runbooks
author: Claire Nguyen
summary: Comprehensive reference for the serving runtime: high-level architecture, kernel & scheduling strategies, profiling/playbook steps, benchmarking suite guide, release notes highlights, known issues, and operational runbooks. This doc is the single-page entry for on-call and engineering teams operating the runtime.
content:
Purpose
-----
This document consolidates the canonical runtime architecture, kernel selection and scheduling policies, profiling and performance playbooks, benchmarking suite guide, core release notes since 2024, a curated known-issues list with mitigations, and operational runbooks for incidents and day-2 tasks. Use this page as the first stop for on-call runbooks and as a reference for runtime-related PRs and design docs.

Audience
--------
Engineers on serving-runtime, infra, SRE, product engineers tuning latency/cost, and support/solutions teams that onboard customers to Dedicated/Private deployments.

High-level architecture overview
-------------------------------
The serving runtime is composed of the following logical services (service names used in configs and dashboards):
- runtime-gateway: HTTP/GRPC ingress, request validation, API auth, routing by customer policy.
- model-router: selects a model variant (float, quantized, fallback) based on policy and availability.
- batcher: continuous batching service that accumulates tokens/requests and emits batched inference jobs.
- kernel-selector: chooses optimized kernels and execution plans per-batch (attention kernel, matmul kernel, fused ops).
- kv-cache: prefix and KV-cache service for conversational sessions; per-customer sharding.
- scheduler: pod-level scheduler that assigns batches to GPU workers respecting locality, GPU memory, and priority.
- tracer and metrics-exporter: distributed tracing, token-level latency metrics, and token cost accounting.
- model-store: artifact store with model binaries and quantization metadata.

Interaction flow (simplified)
1) runtime-gateway authenticates and enriches the request (customer metadata, route policy).
2) model-router picks a target model variant.
3) request enters batcher; batcher produces a batch based on batching policy (max_tokens, max_batch_size, max_wait_ms).
4) kernel-selector compiles/extracts kernel plan for the batch shape and sequence length distribution.
5) scheduler places the batch on a GPU worker; execution is traced and metrics emitted.
6) result is unbatched, post-processed (safety, function calling) and streamed back.

Key SLOs and operational thresholds
----------------------------------
- 95th percentile token latency (hosted API): 120ms token gen for short sequences (<64 tokens).
- 99th percentile token latency: 250ms.
- Inference error rate (5xx or model runtime OOM): <0.2% across production fleet.
- Batch cold-start (kernel plan compile): <50ms median for cached kernel plans; <300ms for on-demand compile.
- KV-cache hit rate target (conversational workloads): >=65% for pinned sessions.
- Scheduler queue depth alert: queue_depth_per_node > 75 for more than 5m.

Kernel selection & scheduling principles
---------------------------------------
Principles:
- Optimize for common-case shapes: short sequences and bursty small requests.
- Prefetch and cache kernel plans for frequent (model, seq_len, dtype) triplets.
- Favor lower-latency single-GPU execution for latency-critical customers; allow multi-GPU sharding for large sequences and throughput-oriented tenants.
- Give priority to SLA customers and routes with lower latency SLOs.

Kernel selection heuristics:
- If (seq_len <= 128 && batch_size <= 16): use fused attention kernel A (float16 fast-path) with continuous KV-cache mode.
- If model is quantized (int4/int8) and hardware supports Q-accel: use quantized matmul + attention kernels and disable layer-norm fusion if numeric instability observed.
- If KV-cache present and request is a continuation: attempt prefix cache hit; if hit, execute delta-only path.

Scheduling policies (high-level)
- Priority classes: real-time (SLA-blessed), interactive (free-tier, hosted), bulk (batch jobs, retraining-like workloads).
- Node packing: prefer colocating same-dtype workloads to reduce kernel warm-up variability.
- Locality: schedule on nodes with warm kernel caches for the model; otherwise prefer lowest GPU memory pressure.
- Preemption: bulk workloads are preemptible; real-time workloads will not be evicted except for critical hardware faults.

Profiling and performance playbook
--------------------------------
When investigating a performance regression, follow this sequence:
1) Verify the alert and scope: check dashboards for latency p50/p95/p99, error-rate, batch size distribution, kv-cache rates, and kernel compile rates.
2) Identify affected cohort: model name/version, customer routes, region, hardware type (A100/MI300/H100).
3) Collect traces: pull trace spans (trace_id from the request or route) and correlate with batcher logs and kernel-selector logs.
4) Check kernel compile churn: high compile rates (>50 compiles/min for a single (model,seq_len,dtype)) indicate insufficient cache pressure.
5) Examine scheduler queueing: long scheduler queue or frequent re-schedules indicate contention or node instability.
6) If OOMs observed, capture worker logs and /var/log/nvidia-smi outputs; check model config (max_seq, activation mem).
7) Apply mitigations: increase kernel-plan cache size, bump batcher max_wait_ms down to reduce variance, or route traffic to a compatible quantized variant as fallback.

Profiling artifacts to collect
- X-Ray/tracing spans (trace-id, timestamps).
- Per-token timing breakdown: tokenize -> enqueue -> batch_wait -> kernel_compile -> kernel_exec -> unbatch -> postproc.
- Kernel planner debug: plan hash, chosen kernels, memory estimates.
- GPU metrics: util, SM%/core occupancy, memory allocated vs resident, PCIe traffic.

Commands and queries (examples)
- Check recent kernel compiles (k8s logs): kubectl -n runtime logs deploy/kernel-selector --since=2h | grep "compile" | tail -n 200
- Query tracing for a trace id: curl -s "https://tracing.internal/api/v1/trace/<TRACE_ID>" | jq .
- Batch distribution query (clickhouse): SELECT bin, count() FROM runtime.batch_events WHERE event_time > now() - interval 1 hour GROUP BY bin ORDER BY bin

Benchmarking suite guide
-----------------------
Purpose: measure latency, throughput, and cost-per-token across model variants, hardware types, and batching policies. The suite is used for onboarding new models, validating kernel improvements, and publishing performance profiles to the model catalog.

Bench components:
- harness: Python-based harness that can simulate route traffic patterns (chatty, chat-burst, long-seq) with configurable concurrency.
- load-generator: k8s job that runs the harness in-cluster for realistic network conditions.
- metrics-collector: aggregates token-level latencies, kernel compile times, GPU counters, and cost estimates.
- report generator: produces HTML and JSON perf profiles consumed by the model catalog.

How to run a standard perf run (short):
1) Checkout repo: git clone git@repo:redwood/serving-runtime-bench.git && cd serving-runtime-bench
2) Configure target: cp configs/example-hosted.yaml configs/run.yaml and set target cluster and credentials.
3) Run: ./bench run --profile chatty --duration 20m --concurrency 50
4) Collect: ./bench collect --output runs/2026-02-12-chatty.json
5) Publish: ./bench publish --run runs/2026-02-12-chatty.json --catalog-model redwood/llama-3b-v1

Bench knobs to capture in reports:
- mean/median/p95/p99 per-token latency
- token throughput (tokens/sec) and tokens per GPU-hour
- kernel compile rate and cold-start impact
- cost per 1M tokens (derived from instance pricing and utilization)

Release notes highlights (runtime-related since 2024)
-------------------------------------------------
- 2024-06: Initial continuous-batching implementation (v1) with online ruler for max_wait_ms.
- 2024-12: Kernel-selector v2 released with fused attention kernels and plan caching; p95 token latency improved ~18% on A100.
- 2025-08: Quantized execution path (int8) GA for selected models; 2.3x cost improvement for throughput workloads.
- 2025-11: Scheduler preemption added and SLA priority classes implemented; reduced tail latencies for real-time customers.
- 2026-01: KV-cache delta-only execution optimized; average token latency improved for long-convo workloads.

Known issues and mitigations (operational)
----------------------------------------
1) Issue: Sudden spike in kernel-plan compiles for a single model variant.
   - Symptom: increased tail latency; logs show many "compile" events.
   - Mitigation: increase kernel-selector cache size (env var KERNEL_CACHE_ENTRIES), or warm kernels by running a lightweight synthetic batcher warm job.

2) Issue: Intermittent OOMs on H100 for long sequences at high concurrency.
   - Symptom: worker restarts, 5xx errors for affected routes.
   - Mitigation: route traffic to float16 multi-GPU sharded variant; reduce per-worker concurrency, enable activation checkpointing for that model.

3) Issue: KV-cache inconsistency after pod restart.
   - Symptom: conversational sessions fall back to full re-eval causing latency spikes.
   - Mitigation: enable sticky session routing (session affinity) and increase kv-cache replication factor to 2 for critical customers.

4) Issue: Quantized path numeric regression on ~0.1% of prompts.
   - Symptom: low-quality output or hallucination surfaced in eval monitors.
   - Mitigation: add model-specific quantization profile exceptions, and route those prompts to full-precision fallback automatically.

Serving runtime operational runbooks
----------------------------------
Runbook: High token-latency alert (p95 token latency > 150ms for > 10 minutes)
1) Triage: identify affected regions/models via dashboard (Runtime > Latency by model).
2) Check batcher metrics: mean batch_size, max_wait_ms, and batch_wait distribution. If batch_wait is high, reduce max_wait_ms for the affected route and scale up batcher replicas.
3) Check kernel-selector: compile rate, cache eviction rate. If compile churn is high, temporarily increase KERNEL_CACHE_ENTRIES and restart kernel-selector with zero-downtime config reload.
4) Check scheduler: node-level queue depth and any node restarts. If a node is unhealthy, cordon it and drain with kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data <node>.
5) Mitigate: if customer SLA impacted, implement traffic split to a compatible quantized model or a capacity pool with reserved GPU nodes (dedicated pool).
6) Post-incident: file a postmortem with timeline, root-cause hypothesis, and corrective actions.

Runbook: Worker OOMs
1) Locate failing pods: kubectl get pods -n runtime | grep OOM
2) Pull logs and kdump: kubectl logs <pod> -n runtime; check /var/log/messages and dmesg for OOM killer entries.
3) If model memory config is mis-specified, rollback config change or patch model.yaml to lower max_seq or disable activations accumulation.
4) If caused by sudden traffic spike, reduce worker concurrency and enable fallback routing to other clusters/variants.
5) Schedule a follow-up: audit model memory estimates and bench on same hardware.

Runbook: Kernel compile storm
1) Identify model/seq_len pairs; check kernel-selector logs for compile hashes.
2) Expand kernel cache (KERNEL_CACHE_ENTRIES) and restart kernel-selector with graceful reload.
3) Pre-warm kernel plans: run bench prewarm --model <model> --seq-lens 8,32,64 --dtype float16 --concurrency 2
4) If new kernel version introduced regression, rollback kernel selector image to previous stable tag.

Appendix: Example model.yaml snippet (config keys used by scheduler and kernel-selector)
---------------------------------------------------------------
model: redwood/llama-3b-v1
dtype: float16
max_seq: 2048
activation_memory_estimate_mb: 8192
batching_policy:
  max_batch_size: 16
  max_wait_ms: 25
  priority_class: interactive
quantization_profiles:
  - name: int8-standard
    enabled: true
    fallback_on_quality_drop: true

(When stored in the model catalog, these keys are read by the scheduler and kernel-selector. If you edit model.yaml, follow PR review and bench runs.)
